sections.title: Display Troubleshooting
sections.content:
NO VIDEO â€” DIAGNOSTIC SEQUENCE.
A system with no video output requires a structured approach. The problem may be in the display, the cable, the GPU, or the driver. Start from the simplest cause.
Step 1: Verify the display has power. Check the power LED. If no LED is lit, check the power cable connection.
Step 2: Check the input source selection. Most displays have multiple inputs â€” HDMI 1, HDMI 2, DisplayPort, VGA. If the wrong input is selected, the display shows no signal even when the PC is outputting correctly. Change input sources manually on the monitor.
Step 3: Inspect the video cable for physical damage. Bent pins, frayed connectors, and damaged shielding cause intermittent or total signal loss. Test with a known-good replacement cable.
Step 4: Test with known-good hardware. Connect the display to a different PC â€” if it displays correctly, the problem is the PC, not the monitor. Connect the PC to a different display â€” if the second display works, the original monitor is at fault.
Step 5: Verify GPU power connectors. Discrete GPUs require 6-pin or 8-pin PCIe power connectors. An unsupported GPU may produce no video output if power connectors are not seated.
Step 6: Check and update video drivers. A corrupt or incompatible video driver can prevent display output. Boot to safe mode â€” which uses the generic Microsoft display driver â€” to verify whether the issue is driver-related.
If POST completes with beep codes but no video appears: the video card is likely not properly seated in the PCIe slot. Reseat it.
DIM IMAGE â€” BACKLIGHT FAILURE.
A display that shows a very dim image â€” barely visible when viewed in a dark room or with a flashlight held against the screen â€” has a functioning panel but a failed backlight. The image is being generated correctly but the backlight that illuminates it is not working.
On older laptops with CCFL â€” Cold Cathode Fluorescent Lamp â€” backlights: CCFL failure or inverter board failure produces this symptom. CCFL backlights require a high-voltage inverter to operate.
On modern LED-backlit displays: an LED driver failure or failed LED strip produces the same symptom.
Backlight failure on a laptop typically requires display assembly service or replacement.
FUZZY OR BLURRY IMAGE.
LCD displays have a fixed native resolution â€” the exact number of pixels in the panel. When configured to run at a resolution other than native â€” for example, 1080p on a 1440p panel â€” the display must scale the image, producing a soft or blurry appearance. Set the resolution to the display's native resolution for a sharp image.
FLICKERING.
Flickering display: check all cable connections â€” even slight looseness causes signal interruptions that appear as flicker. Try a different cable. Check the refresh rate setting â€” some displays do not handle non-standard refresh rates. Persistent flickering with cables confirmed good may indicate a failing GPU or display panel.
DEAD AND STUCK PIXELS.
A dead pixel is a pixel that no longer lights up â€” appears permanently black. A stuck pixel displays one color permanently regardless of what the image shows â€” commonly red, green, or blue.
Dead pixels are panel manufacturing defects. Some manufacturers have a warranty threshold â€” a certain number or pattern of dead pixels must be present before a warranty replacement is provided. Stuck pixels occasionally respond to pixel-exerciser software that rapidly cycles colors.
BURN-IN.
Burn-in is the permanent retention of a static image into the display panel. It is most common on OLED panels and plasma displays because the emissive elements degrade at different rates depending on usage. An image â€” for example, a taskbar or a static logo â€” displayed continuously over many hours causes the corresponding area of the panel to degrade faster than surrounding areas.
Prevention: use screen savers, rotate content displayed, reduce brightness. Once burn-in has occurred it is generally permanent.
COLOR DISTORTION.
Incorrect or shifted colors: check cable connections â€” damaged cable pins can drop color channels. Verify color calibration settings on the monitor and in the OS. Color distortion may also indicate a failing GPU or display panel.
PROJECTOR-SPECIFIC ISSUES.
Projectors use lamps (older models) or LED/laser light sources (modern). Lamp failure in older projectors produces sudden loss of image or a dim purple-tinted image as the lamp degrades. Check bulb hours in the projector's status menu â€” replace before the rated lifespan is exceeded.
Projector overheating shutdowns: blocked ventilation is the most common cause. Keep intake and exhaust vents clear. Allow adequate cool-down time before restarting after a thermal shutdown.
Loose cables produce loss of signal or intermittent signal on projectors just as on direct-connect displays.
---
exam_tips: If you can faintly see an image on an otherwise black display when holding a flashlight to it, the backlight has failed â€” not the panel. The panel is generating an image but the backlight is not illuminating it.

sections.title: Printer Troubleshooting
sections.content:
LASER PRINTER DEFECTS.
Each laser print quality problem maps to a specific component or stage in the laser imaging process. Memorize these mappings â€” they appear on the A+ exam as direct scenario questions.
Faded or light print: low toner is the first suspect. Remove the toner cartridge and gently agitate it to redistribute remaining toner â€” this may temporarily restore output. A worn drum also produces faded output. Replace toner, then drum if toner replacement does not resolve it. Low print density settings in the driver can produce fading without a hardware cause.
Vertical lines or streaks down the page: a scratched or damaged drum surface. The scratch produces a consistent mark at the same horizontal position on every page, appearing as a continuous vertical line. Replace the drum or drum cartridge.
Speckling â€” random spots or dots across the page: toner contamination inside the printer. A toner cartridge that is leaking or a drum assembly that is not cleaning properly distributes loose toner onto the page.
Ghosting â€” double or echo images: a faint secondary image of the previous page content appears on the current page. The drum is not fully discharging between pages, leaving residual charge patterns. This indicates the drum is at or near end of life. Replace the drum.
Smearing or smudging â€” toner that does not fully adhere and rubs off the page: the fuser is not reaching operating temperature and is not permanently bonding the toner to the paper. The fuser assembly requires replacement.
Repetitive marks at consistent intervals: measure the distance between the defect occurrences. If the interval matches the drum's circumference, the defect is on the drum surface. If the interval matches the fuser roller's circumference, the issue is on the fuser roller.
INKJET PRINTER DEFECTS.
Missing lines, horizontal streaks, or incomplete characters: clogged print head nozzles. Dried ink in unused nozzles blocks ink flow. Run the print head cleaning cycle from the printer utility â€” multiple cleaning cycles may be required for severely clogged nozzles. Each cleaning cycle consumes ink.
Wrong colors or color shift: an empty or low cartridge for one color will shift all colors. A clogged nozzle for one color has the same effect. Replace the suspect cartridge or run the cleaning cycle.
Ink smearing on the page: the paper type does not match the ink type. Glossy photo ink on plain paper, or vice versa, produces smearing and poor drying. Verify the paper type setting in the driver matches the actual paper loaded.
PAPER HANDLING FAILURES.
Paper jams: overfilled paper tray â€” reduce paper load. Wrong paper weight or size â€” verify media specifications match the printer's supported types. Worn pickup rollers â€” the rubber rollers that pull paper from the tray wear over time and lose grip. Paper not properly fanned before loading â€” sheets stick together. Humid or damp paper â€” store paper in a dry environment.
Paper not feeding: worn pickup rollers are the primary cause. Check that the paper tray is fully seated and paper guides are adjusted correctly â€” too loose allows skewing, too tight prevents pickup.
Multiple sheets feeding simultaneously: worn separator pad, static buildup on the paper stack, or multiple sheets stuck together. Fan the paper and check the separator pad.
Tray not recognized: verify the tray is fully seated. Check for debris on the tray sensor. Verify the paper size configured in the tray settings matches the actual paper loaded.
PRINT QUEUE AND DRIVER ISSUES.
Print queue frozen: a corrupt print job prevents subsequent jobs from printing. The entire queue appears stuck. Resolution:
1. Stop the Print Spooler service â€” Services.msc or net stop spooler.
2. Navigate to C:\Windows\System32\spool\PRINTERS and delete all files in this folder.
3. Restart the Print Spooler service â€” net start spooler.
Garbled output â€” random characters, symbols, or meaningless text printed instead of the expected document: wrong driver installed. A PCL driver sending jobs to a PostScript printer, or vice versa, produces this symptom. Reinstall the correct driver for the exact printer model and OS version.
Incorrect page orientation â€” portrait job printed in landscape or vice versa: check both the application's print settings and the printer driver's orientation setting. The application setting usually overrides the driver setting.
PRINTER CONNECTIVITY.
USB connectivity: verify the cable is connected at both ends and to the correct USB port. Verify the driver is installed. Test with a different cable.
Network printer connectivity: if the printer's IP address changed â€” from a DHCP lease renewal â€” the configured port on the workstations points to the old address. The fix is to assign the printer a static IP address. Alternatively, configure workstations using the printer's DNS hostname rather than IP address â€” the hostname resolves correctly even if the IP changes.
If the printer shows offline: verify the printer is powered on and network-connected. Check the workstation's printer configuration â€” it may be manually set to offline. Verify no firewall rule is blocking the printing port.
---
exam_tips: Smearing = fuser. Ghosting = drum. Lines = drum scratch. Faded = toner. These four mappings appear directly on the A+ exam as scenario-based questions.

sections.content:

"We covered: IT fundamentals, PC hardware â€” CPU, RAM, storage, motherboards, PSUs, displays, cables, and printers â€” full networking from TCP/IP through DHCP, DNS, Wi-Fi, and troubleshooting â€” mobile devices and enterprise mobility â€” cloud computing and virtualization â€” and hardware and peripheral troubleshooting."
"If you are preparing for the 220-1201 exam: work through these videos, use the shorts for rapid concept review, and put hands on hardware whenever you can. The exam tests what you understand, not what you memorized."
"Subscribe for the Core 2 series when it drops. This is Lab404 â€” signing out."
exam_tips: Garbled or nonsense output from a printer almost always indicates a driver mismatch â€” the wrong driver is installed, or there is a PostScript vs PCL mismatch. Reinstall the correct driver for the specific printer model.

concept_cards.hook: No video on screen doesn't mean the GPU is dead. Work through the sequence â€” the fix is usually the cable, the input source, or the driver.
concept_cards.concept: NO VIDEO, DIM DISPLAY & RESOLUTION ISSUES
concept_cards.summary: No video troubleshooting sequence. Work through these steps in order before assuming hardware failure.

concept_cards.hook: A dead pixel and a stuck pixel are not the same thing. One is permanent. One sometimes responds to treatment. Knowing the difference affects what you tell the customer.
concept_cards.summary: Dead pixels: a pixel that no longer receives a signal and appears permanently black. Dead pixels are a panel manufacturing defect.

concept_cards.hook: Every laser printer defect maps to a specific component. The defect tells you what to replace before you even open the machine.
concept_cards.summary: Laser printer defects follow the imaging process directly â€” each step has a signature failure mode. Faded or light print: insufficient toner on the page.

concept_cards.hook: A frozen print queue that won't clear â€” even after canceling jobs â€” is a Print Spooler service problem. Restarting the service and clearing the spool folder fixes it every time.
concept_cards.concept: PAPER JAMS, PRINT QUEUE, INKJET & GARBLED OUTPUT
concept_cards.summary: Paper jams: most jams are caused by an overfilled tray, incorrect paper weight or type, or worn pickup rollers. Load paper to the tray's fill line, not above it.

practice_questions.q: A monitor displays "No Signal." The PC is powered on and the cable is confirmed secure. What should be checked NEXT?
options: Confirm the correct input source is selected on the monitor

practice_questions.q: A display shows a flickering image. After replacing the video cable with no improvement, what is the NEXT component to suspect?
options: The monitor panel itself or the GPU

practice_questions.q: What is "pixel pitch" in a display specification?
options: The distance between centers of adjacent pixels â€” smaller pitch means a sharper image

practice_questions.q: A laptop screen is black but an external monitor connected via HDMI works fine. What should be checked?
options: Laptop display cable, backlight, or LCD panel

practice_questions.q: What does "dead pixel" mean on a display?
options: A pixel stuck on a bright color permanently
A pixel that never illuminates and remains black regardless of the displayed content
A burnt-in image on the screen
A cluster of bright pixels from overheating

practice_questions.q: A user second monitor shows only a portion of the desktop with the image cut off at edges. What resolves this?
options: Overscan or underscan setting adjustment, or correcting the display resolution

practice_questions.q: What is the FIRST thing to check when a projector displays "no signal"?
options: Confirm the correct input source is selected and the cable is connected

practice_questions.q: A monitor displays in portrait orientation when it should be landscape. What is the fix?
options: Adjust display orientation in Windows display settings

practice_questions.q: What GPU temperature range is generally considered acceptable under full load for most consumer graphics cards?
options: 70-85 degrees C (above 95 degrees is a concern for most cards)

practice_questions.q: A projector image appears trapezoidal rather than rectangular. What adjustment corrects this?
What is the MOST common reason an HDMI monitor connected to a laptop shows no signal even with a good cable?
options: Display output mode not configured â€” use Win+P to select the correct display mode

practice_questions.q: What does refresh rate measure in a display?
options: Make the image appear blurry or stretched due to upscaling interpolation
Make the image sharper due to larger pixels
Not affect image quality at all

practice_questions.q: A GPU shows artifacting on screen with normal temperatures. After testing with a different monitor and same result, what is MOST likely?
options: Driver corruption or failing GPU VRAM

practice_questions.q: A laser printer produces pages where the toner smears or rubs off easily. The MOST likely failing component is:
A printer produces a blank page every time it prints. The FIRST thing to check is:
options: Toner or ink level, and whether protective tape was removed from a new cartridge

practice_questions.q: What does the Windows print spooler service do?
options: Physically routes cables to the printer
Manages and queues print jobs between applications and the printer

practice_questions.q: A laser printer produces a repeating smudge or mark at regular intervals on every page. The MOST likely cause is:
options: Contamination or damage on the drum or rollers at the interval matching the drum circumference
practice_questions.explanation: Repeating defects at regular intervals are caused by a contaminated or damaged component that repeats on every rotation. The interval distance equals the circumference of the offending part. Drum circumference (~94 mm for a typical cartridge) repeats every ~3.7 inches. If the interval is shorter, su

practice_questions.q: What does "toner scatter" appearing as speckles around text on laser-printed pages typically indicate?
options: Damaged drum, high humidity, or incorrect paper type

practice_questions.q: A network printer worked yesterday but shows offline today with no known changes. The FIRST thing to check is:
options: Verify the printer IP address has not changed due to DHCP lease expiration

practice_questions.q: What causes "ghosting" on a laser-printed page â€” a faint duplicate image offset from the main image?
options: Worn drum unit that is not fully discharging residual charge after the transfer step
practice_questions.explanation: Drum ghosting: a worn drum retains residual charge from a prior print cycle, attracting toner in that same pattern on subsequent pages, creating a faint ghost of an earlier image.
